issues.issue: This legend flatly prohibits any reproduction or distribution of the Memorandum without the Manager's prior written consent, while the CONFIDENTIAL/TRADE SECRET legend (c011) expressly permits the recipient to distribute it to his own financial and legal advisors. A court would have to decide which of the two permission regimes governs a disclosure to advisors.

The legend requires investors to rely solely on their own examination of the Notes and the offering, whereas the Conflicts of Interest sections (c038, c050) state that Noteholders 'must rely on the good faith and integrity of the Manager.' The two allocations of reliance cannot easily be given effect together in a misrepresentation dispute.

This legend states categorically that the Company 'will not be registered as an investment company,' while the Risk Factor 'Company Not Registered' (c206) admits there is no assurance the Company will not become subject to the Investment Company Act. Whether the legend is a promise or merely a present expectation is left open.

The legend permits transfer 'except as provided in the Note Purchase Agreement referred to herein,' but the Note Purchase Agreement (§7) forbids all transfers absent the Company's consent while the Memorandum's 'Transfers of Notes' term (c124) carves out family trusts, wholly-owned affiliates and operation of law. The permitted-transfer set therefore differs depending on which document is read.

The Company's undertaking to furnish additional information is bounded only by what it can obtain 'without unreasonable effort or expense,' a standard the Memorandum nowhere defines or measures. The scope of the disclosure obligation therefore has no ascertainable boundary.

The sentence is joined by a comma splice ('THE COMPANY BELIEVES THAT SUCH INFORMATION IS ACCURATE ..., THE COMPANY CANNOT GUARANTEE THE ACCURACY'), so it reads as both an affirmation and a disclaimer of the same third-party data. The punctuation makes it unclear whether any representation of accuracy is being made at all.

The Manager and its affiliates reserve the right to modify any term of the offering and the Offering Documents before the final closing, which cannot be squared with 'Amendments, Waivers of Noteholder Agreements' (c131) requiring the written approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders for any modification of the Note Purchase Agreement, Notes or Security Agreement. A court would have to decide which controls for a Noteholder whose Note is issued at an earlier closing.

'We may terminate this offering at any time before a closing' does not say whether 'a closing' means the Initial Closing or any of the successive closings contemplated by the Closing term (c109), so the termination right's expiry date is indeterminate. The singular article gives the sentence two reasonable readings.

This legend allows the recipient to consult and give copies to his own financial and legal advisors, whereas the opening confidentiality legend (c001) prohibits reproduction or distribution 'in whole or in part' without the Manager's prior written consent. The two confidentiality undertakings impose inconsistent duties on the same recipient.

The Executive Summary states without qualification that 'The Notes will be secured by the assets of the Company,' but the Use of capital paragraph (c019) and the Company Borrowings term (c125) permit borrowings secured by liens senior to the lien securing the Notes. Whether investors were promised a first-priority security interest is left to be construed from the two passages together.

The offer of 'superior returns with a conservative risk profile' and a target of 'approximately 8.00% or more per year' conflicts with the Risk Factors' statement that the purchase of Notes involves a high degree of risk and that investors must be able to lose their entire investment (c169, c207). A court could be asked whether the summary's characterization is a term of the bargain or mere puffery displaced by the risk section.

The stated purpose confines Portfolio Loans to commercial real estate and related purposes 'throughout the United States,' but the Geographic Area of Lending Activity provision (c059) permits up to 20% of Company capital to be lent on non-U.S. properties and the General Standards (c056) permit residential construction loans. The scope of permitted lending differs depending on which provision governs.

This paragraph says the Manager only 'expects to hire' Bar-K, Inc. as Servicer, whereas the Bar-K, Inc., the Servicer section (c030) states that the Manager 'has selected' Bar-K and the Servicer term (c084) makes Bar-K the initial Servicer. Whether the engagement of the affiliate Servicer was already fixed is left in doubt.

The Summary says closings are expected on the first day of each calendar month 'through May 1, 2009,' while the Closing term (c109) sets the final closing at the last day of the sixth full quarter after the Initial Closing (estimated June 30, 2009) and the Note Purchase Agreement (§2.1) contemplates quarterly closings. The end of the subscription period and the closing frequency cannot be reconciled across the three statements.

The Summary promises 'a minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized,' whereas the Floating Rate term (c089) and Note Purchase Agreement §1.3 impose a floor of 8% for each calendar year rather than an average. A rate averaging 8% but falling below 8% in some quarters would satisfy one provision and breach the other.

This paragraph states that a Noteholder may request prepayment after holding the Note one year, omitting the further conditions imposed by the Return of Investment term (c103) and Note Purchase Agreement §1.4(a)(ii) — sixty days' notice and a quarter-end effective date. Which set of conditions governs a prepayment request must be construed.

The statement that Noteholders 'will be secured creditors of the Company' sits against the Use of capital paragraph (c019) and Failure of Security risk factor (c200), which permit the Noteholders' security interest to be subordinated to Company Borrowings and give no assurance of perfection. The quality of the creditor status conferred is only ascertainable by reading those provisions together.

This paragraph permits borrowings secured by liens on Company assets 'senior to the lien securing the Notes,' which cannot be squared with the Executive Summary's unqualified statement that the Notes will be secured by the assets of the Company (c012) and that Noteholders are secured creditors (c018). A court would have to decide whether the senior-lien authority qualifies the security promise.

The covenant that the Company 'will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market and will not source loans for the purpose of resale' cannot be squared with Credit Evaluations (c063), which expressly permits loans to borrowers in default on other obligations or without qualifying income, and with Sale of Loans Generally (c078), which permits occasional resale. What counts as sub-prime lending or sourcing for resale would have to be construed against those provisions.

The assertion that 'no investor has experienced a loss of investment principal through investment vehicles sponsored by the Principals' is an unqualified historical representation that the projections disclaimer (c026) purports to reduce to illustration only. Whether the track-record statement survives that disclaimer as a representation is open.

The description of R.E. Loans' $750 million portfolio and 8.5% average investor returns says nothing of R.E. Loans' secured credit facility, the Loan and Security Agreement with Wells Fargo Foothill dated July 17, 2007 filed in this case, under which its notes receivable were pledged. Read with that instrument, the portrayal of the affiliate whose loans the Company expects to buy (c055) is materially incomplete.

The claim that Bar-K 'has a 100% collection record with respect to loans it administers' sits against the Sale of Defaulted Loans provisions (c053, c077) and the tax discussion (c151), which describe the affiliates' practice of buying defaulting loans out of the fund. Whether a collection record achieved by affiliate repurchase is what the sentence represents would have to be construed.

This disclaimer treats everything said about prior results as 'historical only' and 'for illustration purposes,' which cannot readily be squared with the specific affirmative claims in Investor Opportunities (c022) and Bar-K servicing (c025) that no investor has lost principal and that Bar-K has a 100% collection record. A court would have to decide whether the disclaimer negates those representations.

This section states that the four members of B-4 Partners LLC are Walter Ng, Bruce Horwitz, Barney Ng and Kelly Ng, while Other Funds or Businesses (c047) describes B-4 Partners LLC as 'owned and managed by Walter Ng and Dr. Bruce Horwitz.' The ownership of the affiliate that manages R.E. Loans is stated two different ways.

The sentence describes Bar-K as 'a real estate broker licensed by the California Department of Corporations,' mismatching the licence to the licensing agency (real estate brokers are licensed by the Department of Real Estate; finance lenders by the Department of Corporations). The error clouds what licences the Servicer actually holds, a point the Lending Laws discussion (c165, c166) makes material.

'The Servicer will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company' cannot be squared with the Manager's right to retain other firms in lieu of the Servicer (c042) or with Purchase of Loans from Servicer (c072), which allows purchases from unrelated third parties. Whether the Servicer has an exclusive origination role is left in doubt.

The Manager's reserved right to terminate all or any portion of its business relationship with the Company 'at any time' conflicts with Restricted Actions (c126) and Note Purchase Agreement §6.2(e), which bar withdrawal of the sole manager without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. The two provisions give opposite answers to whether the Manager may walk away unilaterally.

This paragraph makes the payee of Loan Services compensation turn on whether the Company or the Manager contracts with the Servicer, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.4 makes all such fees payable to the Manager (or its designee) in every case. Which document determines who is entitled to the Loan Servicing Fee must be resolved.

The paragraph opens by stating that under Delaware law a manager is accountable to the company's members as a fiduciary, then concludes that the Manager has no fiduciary obligation to the Company's members because it is itself the sole member. The passage both asserts and disclaims the same duty, leaving the Manager's actual duty to be construed.

This paragraph states the indemnity and exculpation standard as 'fraud, bad faith or willful misconduct,' while the Exculpation and Indemnification term (c132) and Note Purchase Agreement §5.5(c) state it as 'willful misconduct or gross negligence.' Grossly negligent conduct is indemnified under one formulation and not the other.

Requiring Noteholders to 'rely on the good faith and integrity of the Manager' is difficult to square with the same section's conclusion (c034) and Note Purchase Agreement §4.3 that the Manager owes the Noteholders no fiduciary or similar duty. Whether any enforceable good-faith obligation is created by this sentence is open.

The closing cross-reference is to '(See "Fiduciary Responsibility of the Managing Member.")', a section that does not exist in the Memorandum — the corresponding heading is 'No Fiduciary Responsibility of Manager to Noteholders' (c034), and 'Managing Member' is nowhere defined. The reader is pointed to a provision that cannot be located.

The brokerage, renewal and forbearance fees the Servicer may charge Portfolio Borrowers are described only as anticipated to be 'in the amount set forth herein' but 'may be higher or lower depending upon market conditions,' with no ceiling. The provision states a figure and then removes any boundary on it.

The Manager's right to retain other firms 'in lieu of the Servicer' conflicts with the statement that the Servicer 'will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company' (c031) and with the Servicer term (c084) naming Bar-K as Servicer. Whether Bar-K's role is exclusive or displaceable must be construed.

'Related Party Loans' is defined here as loans to persons affiliated with the Manager, Members or Servicer, but Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e) defines the term by reference to 'Affiliate' and expressly excludes loans to Sponsored Investment Funds and Private Clients. The class of loans subject to the related-party limits differs between the two documents.

This limit is 20% of total Company assets 'at any time,' whereas the parallel Portfolio Loan Criteria provision (c071) tests the 20% only 'upon the closing of the Related Party Loan in question' and Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e)(ii) measures 20% of the Loan Portfolio immediately after making the loan. A continuous covenant and a point-in-time test on different denominators cannot both be applied.

The condition requires Related Party Loans to be consistent with 'the lending standards and policies set forth above,' but no lending standards appear above this point in the Memorandum — they are set out later in Section IV (c056–c063). The referent of 'set forth above' cannot be identified.

This provision requires the Manager to purchase a defaulted Related Party Loan 'at par,' while Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e)(iii) fixes the price at no less than outstanding principal plus accrued interest. The two formulas produce different prices where interest has accrued, and 'material event of default' is left undefined in both.

The Manager's allocation of loan opportunities between the Company and Other Sponsored Investment Funds is governed only by 'consideration of all relevant factors, including' an open list, which sets no standard a Noteholder could enforce. The catch-all swallows the enumerated factors of loan size, diversification, remaining term and uncommitted capital.

The direction that Noteholders 'must rely on the Manager to act in good faith' sits against the express disclaimer of any fiduciary or similar duty to Noteholders (c034 and Note Purchase Agreement §4.3). Whether this sentence creates an obligation or merely describes the investors' predicament is unresolved.

The Manager and Principals are to devote 'only so much time to the business of the Company as is reasonably required,' a measure with no stated benchmark and no minimum. The commitment cannot be tested against anything in the Memorandum.

The Manager's obligation on a defaulted loan is that its 'first priority will usually be' to obtain full recovery 'or so much thereof as can reasonably be obtained in light of current market conditions' — 'usually' and 'reasonably' leave the duty without any fixed content. It is unclear whether any enforceable obligation is created at all.

This provision sets an affiliate purchase price 'not less than' the independently appraised value, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(b)(ii) requires a price 'no higher than the independently appraised value of such property at the time of sale.' The two documents impose opposite constraints against the same appraisal figure.

'A purchase price ... which is not less than any of the following: (i) ... (ii) ... or (iii)' is ambiguous between a price at or above the highest of the three measures and a price at or above any one of them. The disjunctive 'any ... or' makes the pricing floor indeterminate.

This paragraph states that purchases from and co-investments with R.E. Loans will comply with 'lending criteria for such loans established by the Note Purchase Agreement,' but Note Purchase Agreement §5.3(e) permits the Company to buy and sell Portfolio Loans from Sponsored Investment Funds 'on such terms and conditions as the Manager, in its sole discretion, determines.' Whether any criteria in fact constrain these affiliate transactions must be construed.
